say.en: A company can sell shares, borrow from the public, take a bank loan or simply keep its profits. Each source has a different cost, risk and control. In this lesson: Classify sources of finance by period and ownership.
Explain equity shares, preference shares, retained earnings and debentures.
Compare owners' funds with borrowed funds.

body.en: *Owners' funds* are provided by the owners and are not repaid during the life of the business. Equity shares carry ownership and voting rights; equity shareholders take the risk and receive dividends only if profits allow, so equity is permanent capital with no fixed burden. Preference shares get a fixed rate of dividend before equity shareholders and preference in the return of capital on winding up, but usually no voting rights. Retained earnings (ploughing back of profits) are an internal source with no cost of issue, but they reduce dividends and depend on profits.

points.en: Preference: fixed dividend, priority, usually no vote
Retained earnings: internal, no issue cost
Not repayable during the life of the firm

say.en: A company needs 100 rupees lakh. It can raise part by debt at a fixed interest rate and the rest by equity. If its return on investment is higher than the interest rate, more debt raises the profit available per rupee of equity.

body.en: *Owners' funds* give permanent capital, no fixed burden and no charge on assets, but dilute control and are costly because shareholders expect a higher return for their risk. Borrowed funds do not dilute control, interest is tax-deductible, and when the return on investment exceeds the interest rate they raise the return to shareholders (trading on equity); but interest must be paid even in loss, repayment is compulsory, and too much debt increases financial risk. A sound firm balances the two.

Trading on equity when ROI > interest

problem.en: A company earns ₹30 lakh before interest on capital of ₹200 lakh. Plan A: all equity. Plan B: ₹100 lakh equity and ₹100 lakh debentures at 10%. Compare the return on equity (ignore tax).

steps.en: Plan A: profit for equity = ₹30 lakh on ₹200 lakh = 15%.
Plan B: interest = 10% of 100 = ₹10 lakh; profit for equity = ₹20 lakh.
Since ROI (15%) > interest (10%), debt raises the return to shareholders.

answer.en: Plan A 15%, Plan B 20%: trading on equity benefits shareholders.

say.en: A company earns 30 rupees lakh before interest on capital of 200 rupees lakh. Plan A: all equity. Plan B: 100 rupees lakh equity and 100 rupees lakh debentures at 10 percent. Compare the return on equity ignore tax.
Plan A: profit for equity equals 30 rupees lakh on 200 rupees lakh equals 15 percent.
Plan B: interest equals 10 percent of 100 equals 10 rupees lakh; profit for equity equals 20 rupees lakh.
Return on equity equals 20 divided by 100 equals 20 percent.
Since ROI 15 percent is greater than interest 10 percent, debt raises the return to shareholders.
So the answer is Plan A 15 percent, Plan B 20 percent: trading on equity benefits shareholders.
